Complete Empirical Research Plan  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Random-assignment–based Instrumental Variables (IV) design.

•  Within each of the 78 teacher pairs the district decided by coin-flip whether to swap the two pre-constructed class rosters.  
•  Because rosters are constructed to be ex-ante equivalent and the swap decision is centrally random, the indicator “roster swap” is an exogenous instrument for whether a given student is taught by the higher ex-ante value-added (VA) teacher.  
•  First, use this random instrument to obtain the causal impact of being taught by a teacher whose non-experimental VA is one standard deviation higher.  
•  Second, compare the experimental (IV) estimate to the coefficient from an OLS regression that uses the same VA measure but ignores the instrument.  A slope of one in the IV-on-OLS comparison implies the non-experimental VA is unbiased.  
•  Third, follow students for up to two later grades and estimate the IV effect on future test scores to measure persistence.

This approach is superior to DiD or RDD because the main variation—the roster swap—is an explicit randomized experiment that cleanly satisfies the relevance and exogeneity requirements for IV.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
    T_i = 1 if student i is taught by the teacher in her pair whose pre-period non-experimental VA exceeds her partner’s (High-VA teacher).  

Control group  
    Students assigned to the lower-VA teacher within the same pair (T_i = 0).

Instrument  
    Z_i = 1 if the district swapped the two rosters in the pair; 0 otherwise.  
    By construction, Z_i ⟂ potential outcomes within pair.

Treatment timing  
    The treatment occurs at the beginning of the school year (September 2003 or 2004). End-of-year tests in spring provide the primary outcome; spring tests in t+1 and t+2 provide persistence outcomes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Random assignment (instrument exogeneity) – Students’ potential test scores are independent of Z_i within each pair.  
    • Plausible: central computerized coin-flip; principals can neither observe nor influence the decision.

A2. First-stage relevance – Z_i strongly predicts T_i (swapping rosters flips which roster gets the higher-VA teacher).  
    • Plausible: compliance rate 85 %; the instrument should generate a sizable first stage.

A3. Monotonicity – No student would receive the higher-VA teacher when swap = 0 but the lower-VA teacher when swap = 1 (no “defiers”).  
    • Plausible: because the swap simply exchanges entire rosters, individual students cannot selectively move in the opposite direction.

A4. Exclusion – Z_i affects outcomes only through the identity/quality of the teacher, not via classroom peers because rosters are pre-balanced.  
    • Plausible given principals created equivalent rosters; will be probed with balance and peer-composition checks.

A5. SUTVA – One student’s potential outcome is unaffected by which teacher other students in the pair receive, aside from within-classroom peer effects common to the treatment.  
    • Partially plausible; we will show peer covariates do not differentially change with Z_i.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Non-compliance & Mid-year transfers (15 % leave assigned teacher)  
   – Define treatment as “assigned to high-VA teacher” and keep IV framework (LATE applies to compliers).  
   – Check robustness by (i) restricting to stayers, (ii) estimating bounds à la Lee (2009).

2. Differential attrition from the testing sample  
   – Compare attrition rates and observable characteristics by Z_i.  
   – Use inverse-probability weighting and Lee bounds if necessary.

3. Miss-measurement of pre-period VA (sampling error)  
   – Split-sample shrinkage estimator for VA (Kane & Staiger 2008 style).  
   – Correct standard errors for VA estimation error using a two-stage jackknife or bootstrapping.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)       # fast data
library(fixest)           # high-dim FE + IV
library(marginaleffects)  # delta method for persistence
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Load and merge data
stud <- fread("lausd_student_panel.csv")      # student-year panel
teacher_va <- fread("teacher_preperiod_VA.csv")  # VA estimates 1999-2003
pairs <- fread("teacher_pairs.csv")           # pair_id, highVA_teacher_id, year, swap

# 2. Create analysis sample (2003-04 & 2004-05 cohorts only)
df <- merge(stud, pairs, by = c("pair_id","year"))
df <- merge(df, teacher_va, by = "teacher_id", all.x = TRUE)

# 3. Key variables
df[, highVA := (teacher_id == highVA_teacher_id)]  # T_i
df[, swap := swap]                                 # Z_i
df[, outcome_0 := test_std]                        # same-year score
df[, outcome_1 := lead(test_std, 1), by = student_id]  # t+1
df[, outcome_2 := lead(test_std, 2), by = student_id]  # t+2

# 4. Baseline covariates (lagged scores, demographics)
covars <- c("lag_math_std","lag_read_std","female","frl","ell","black",
            "hispanic","asian","gifted","sped")

# 5. Main 2SLS specification
form1 <- as.formula(paste0(
  "outcome_0 ~ ", paste(covars,"collapse = +"),
  " | pair_id + grade + year | ",
  " highVA ~ swap | 0"     # 0 for no additional cluster FE
))

est_main <- feols(form1, data = df, cluster = "pair_id")

# 6. Persistence (outcome_1, outcome_2)
form_p1 <- update(form1, outcome_1 ~ .)
form_p2 <- update(form1, outcome_2 ~ .)

est_p1 <- feols(form_p1, data = df, cluster = "pair_id")
est_p2 <- feols(form_p2, data = df, cluster = "pair_id")

# 7. Robustness – add classroom peer controls
peer_vars <- c("class_mean_lag_read","class_sd_lag_read",
               "class_share_frl","class_share_ell")
form_rb <- update(form1, paste(". ~ . +", paste(peer_vars, collapse="+")))
est_rb <- feols(form_rb, data = df, cluster = "pair_id")

# 8. Summarize
modelsummary(list(Main = est_main, PeerRobust = est_rb,
                  Persist1 = est_p1, Persist2 = est_p2),
             stars = TRUE, gof_omit = "Adj|AIC|BIC",
             output = "results_table.html")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
•  Same-year impact: A 1-SD increase in teacher VA should raise student test scores by roughly 0.20–0.25 SD (consistent with prior estimates for grades 2–5).  
•  Persistence: About 40 % of the initial gain remains in t+1 (≈0.08-0.10 SD) and 20 % in t+2.  
•  Unbiasedness test: The slope from regressing experimental effects on predicted VA differences is expected to be close to 1; i.e., non-experimental VA is approximately unbiased.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Relevance (first-stage F-stat > 10) ................. 1  
C2: Independence / Randomization verified ............... 1  
C3: Exclusion restriction plausible & tested ............ 0.8  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ............................ 1  
C5: Stable unit treatment value (limited spillovers) ..... 0.7  

Overall: 4.5 / 5 – strong but peer-effect spillovers and attrition remain possible concerns.
